content:
"Coming Out of the Ice" is a 1982 made-for-television film that tells the harrowing true story of Victor Herman, an American who spent 18 years in Soviet labor camps (gulags) during Stalin's era.

**The Story:**
- Based on Victor Herman's autobiography of the same name
- Herman was the son of Jewish-American Communists who moved to the Soviet Union in 1931 when he was 16, believing in the Communist ideal
- He became a celebrated parachutist and was known as "The Eagle of the Soviet Union"
- In 1938, during Stalin's purges, he was arrested on false charges and sentenced to 10 years in labor camps
- After his sentence, he was forced to remain in Siberian exile for another 8 years
- He eventually married a fellow prisoner and had a daughter
- Finally allowed to return to the US in 1976 after decades of struggle

**The Film:**
- Starred John Savage as Victor Herman
- Also featured Willie Nelson in a supporting role as a fellow prisoner
- Ben Cross played another prisoner
- Directed by Waris Hussein
- Aired on CBS as a TV movie
- The film depicted the brutal conditions of the Soviet gulag system

**Historical Significance:**
The story provided Western audiences with a personal account of the Soviet labor camp system during a time when Cold War tensions were still high and information about life behind the Iron Curtain was limited.

The film and book helped raise awareness about the experiences of Americans and other foreigners who were caught up in Stalin's purges and the broader human rights abuses of the Soviet system.
